articles.title: Panic attack or anxiety attack: what it feels like, what to do, and when it is something else
sources: NHS, "Anxiety, fear and panic" (Open Government Licence)
NHS, "Panic disorder" (Open Government Licence)
NIMH (National Institute of Mental Health), "Panic Disorder: What You Need to Know"
MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine), "Panic Disorder" health topic
VA National Center for PTSD, "Coping with Traumatic Stress Reactions"
MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine), "Hyperventilation" (medical encyclopedia)
SAMHSA, "Tips for Survivors of a Disaster or Other Traumatic Event: Managing Stress" (SMA13-4776)
FEMA, CERT Basic Training Participant Manual (2019), Unit 5, "Disaster Psychology"
guidance: People say "anxiety attack" and "panic attack" for the same thing: a sudden wave of intense fear or discomfort, or a feeling of losing control, that comes on fast, often for no clear reason and even when there is no danger. It can happen at any time, even during sleep. It peaks, and it passes: most last 5 to 20 minutes, a few up to an hour. Frightening as it is, a panic attack is not dangerous and does not physically harm you.

What it feels like: a racing or pounding heart, sweating, trembling or shaky limbs, shortness of breath or breathing very fast, a choking feeling, chest pain, nausea or a churning stomach, feeling faint or dizzy, chills or hot flushes, numbness or tingling in the fingers or lips, a dry mouth, feeling unreal or not connected to your own body, and a sense of dread or a fear of dying or of losing control. It can feel exactly like a heart attack, which is why it is so frightening.

Much of what the body is doing comes from breathing too fast. Fast, deep breathing lowers the carbon dioxide in the blood, and that by itself brings on the lightheaded, spacey feeling, the pounding heart, and the sense of not being able to catch a breath. The thoughts that ride along with it, "I am dying", "this is a heart attack", "I am losing control", are what make it so upsetting, and they are not true. The sensations pass soon, and slowing the breathing helps them pass.

If it is you: stay where you are, if you can. Breathe slowly and deeply, in through the nose and out through the mouth, and make the out-breath the long one: pursing the lips as if blowing out a candle and letting the air out slowly does it. Remind yourself that this is a panic attack, that it will pass, and that it is not life-threatening. Put your mind on something peaceful and calming. See Slow breathing: the calming exercise for stress, anxiety, and panic.

If it is someone else: the calm in your voice is the treatment. Stay with them, keep your voice soft, low, and unhurried, and say the true things: "You are doing fine. You are not having a heart attack. You are not going to die. This passes." Then help them slow their breathing: count with them, in for a slow count of five and out for a slow count of five, and breathe that way yourself so they have something to copy. Ask before you touch them or move them. "Snap out of it" and "get control of yourself" do not help; they only tell the person they are failing. Do not argue with what they are feeling.

When it is not panic. Rapid breathing for the first time in someone's life may be a medical emergency and is a reason to get them to care right away. So is pain, a fever, or bleeding along with it, and so is breathing trouble that continues or gets worse despite the steps above. A racing heart can also come from low blood pressure and other conditions, and nearly every symptom on the list can belong to something else. If you are not sure, do not assume panic: treat chest pain as the heart until proven otherwise (see Chest pain: sorting the causes, and treating it as the heart until proven otherwise, and Heart attack and aspirin boundaries) and get medical help by whatever route actually works: call if you have signal, otherwise get them there or send someone.

Afterward: attacks are more likely when the body is run down. Regular meals keep energy steady; sugary food and drinks, caffeine, alcohol, and smoking all make attacks worse; exercise, even a walk, and daily breathing practice reduce them; talking to someone about it helps. Someone who keeps having attacks and has spent a month or more worrying about the next one has panic disorder, which is common and treatable with talking therapy and medicine. See a provider when one can be reached.

Anxiety that is not an attack, the slow kind: tense, unable to relax, worrying about the past or the future, tearful, not sleeping, unable to concentrate, fearing the worst, a heartbeat you notice, headaches, an upset stomach, and avoiding the places and situations that bring it on. It is common after a disaster (see Stress reactions after a disaster: what is normal, what helps, and when to get help). What helps: talk about how you feel to someone you trust; move your body; eat regular meals; use the breathing exercise; set small targets rather than trying to do everything at once; put your energy into what you can change, not what you cannot; do not avoid what makes you anxious, build up to it slowly; and do not reach for alcohol, cigarettes, or drugs, which make it worse. If it is not easing, or it is stopping you living, that is a reason to get help.

articles.title: Slow breathing: the calming exercise for stress, anxiety, and panic
sources: NHS, "Breathing exercises for stress" (Open Government Licence)
VA National Center for PTSD, "Coping with Traumatic Stress Reactions"
MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine), "Hyperventilation" (medical encyclopedia)
SAMHSA, "Tips for Survivors of a Disaster or Other Traumatic Event: Managing Stress" (SMA13-4776)
guidance: This is the NHS's calming breathing exercise for stress, anxiety, and panic. It takes a few minutes and can be done anywhere: standing, sitting in a chair that supports your back, or lying down. It works best when it is practised every day, so that the body already knows it when the bad moment comes.

Get as comfortable as you can and loosen anything that restricts your breathing. Lying down: arms a little away from your sides, palms up, legs straight or knees bent with the feet flat. Sitting: arms on the chair arms. Sitting or standing: both feet flat on the ground, roughly hip-width apart.

Let the breath flow as deep down into the belly as is comfortable, without forcing it. Breathe in through the nose and out through the mouth. Breathe in gently and steadily, counting from 1 to 5 if that helps; you may not reach 5 at first, and that is fine. Then let the breath flow out gently, counting from 1 to 5 again. Keep going for at least 5 minutes.

In a panic attack, the out-breath is the part that matters. Pursing the lips as if blowing out a candle and letting the air out slowly is how to let the body's carbon dioxide come back up, which ends most of the symptoms. Learning to breathe from the belly, rather than the upper chest, does the same over time.

Reading it to someone: sit or kneel where they can see you, keep your voice low and slow, and count with them, "In, two, three, four, five. Out, two, three, four, five," breathing the same way yourself so they have something to copy. A pounding heart and a spacey, lightheaded feeling usually come from fast breathing and are not dangerous, and each time the breathing slows and the sensations pass, the next attack has a little less hold.

A caution from the VA: for a few people, paying close attention to the body's sensations makes distress worse at first. If that happens, keep the practice short, and mix it with walking, music, or something else that keeps them in touch with the world around them; small amounts that can be handled still help.

The deep breath before each task: after a disaster, a few deep breaths, or a gentle stretch, before you start each job on the list is the simplest way to keep the stress from stacking up through the day, and deep breathing can even stop a panic attack from taking hold.

articles.title: Calming someone who is falling apart: psychological first aid
sources: U.S. Army, ATP 4-02.11 First Aid (March 2026), chapter 20, "Combat and Operational Stress Control"
FEMA, CERT Basic Training Participant Manual (2019), Unit 5, "Disaster Psychology"
National Child Traumatic Stress Network and National Center for PTSD, "Psychological First Aid: Field Operations Guide", 2nd edition (2006)
SAMHSA, "Tips for Survivors of a Disaster or Other Traumatic Event: Managing Stress" (SMA13-4776)
guidance: Psychological first aid is as real as the bandage kind. Fear and anxiety can take as much out of a person as blood loss, and a frightened person does not respond to joking, indifference, or fearful, tearful attention. Everyone who is injured is also upset about being injured; the worse the injury, or the more that part of the body matters to them, the more frightened and insecure they become, and the fear can make them irritable, uncooperative, or unreasonable. It has nothing to do with you. They need patience, reassurance, encouragement, and support.

What it looks like when stress is getting past someone: trembling, tearfulness, jumpiness, a cold sweat and a dry mouth, a pounding heart, dizziness, nausea, exhaustion, a thousand-yard stare, trouble thinking or getting words out, indecision, forgetfulness, irritability, being startled by every noise, grief, anger, and a loss of confidence. Most or all of these can be present in a perfectly normal person under enough strain, and with encouragement most people carry on. The trouble is when they can no longer do what needs doing.

Medical needs come first, then the mind. Look at how responsive they are and whether they are a danger to themselves or anyone else. Then stay calm yourself, because nothing frightens an upset person more than sensing that others are afraid of them. If they can see your calm, your confidence, and that you expect them to come through this, they will feel safer.

Take them as they are. Do not blame them, ridicule them, or make light of how they feel; a person does not want to be upset, and when they reach for help they need consideration of their fears, not dismissal. "It's all in your head", "snap out of it", and "get control of yourself" are not help; they are hostility that only emphasises weakness. Nobody expects a person with a badly sprained ankle to run. An overwhelmed mind is a disability just as real, and some people cannot simply pull themselves together on demand.

Bring the familiar back. Use their name. Hand them a cup of coffee or water; see to a small cut; put them within sight of people and things they know. Speak in clear, simple sentences and repeat them. Tell them what is happening and what is being done to keep everyone safe, and stop rumours. Let them know that the reaction they are having is normal and that there is nothing seriously wrong with them.

Let them talk. Ask them to tell you, in their own words, what happened, and be a good listener; do not force it, and do not argue with how they see it, even to put it in perspective. Let them know you are willing to listen whenever they want, and check back. If they become overwhelmed, suggest a break and promise to listen again as soon as they are ready. Going over it, in talk and in dreams, is how people master a frightening event, and it is not a sign of something wrong.

Then give them something to do. Fear eases with activity: a useful, simple job, with clear directions on what to do and where. Sorting supplies, carrying water, minding a child, keeping a list. This is especially the answer for someone who is disruptive. It puts their thoughts somewhere productive, gives the tension an outlet, and proves to them that they can still do something. Do not let them just sit. As they steady, bring them back into the group, because a person handles danger far better inside a close group than alone.

See to the body. Exhaustion is often the real cause of an emotional collapse. A safe, dry, quiet place to sleep, food, water, and a wash with clean clothes do more than any words. Make sure they eat, drink, and sleep as soon as possible.

Watch your own feelings. Tired and worried, you will be tempted to be impatient with someone who is slow or over the top, even to resent them; that shows, and it hurts. The opposite, drowning them in pity, hurts too: they need strong help, not your sorrow. Expect them to recover and to be useful again, and let that show in what you say and do. Experience with police, firefighters, and medics shows that doing this for everyone involved, including the people who coped well, greatly cuts the odds of lasting harm.

If they are frozen, dazed, wandering, or out of control, see Someone who is frozen, dazed, wandering, or out of control. If they say they want to die, see When someone says they want to die. For the words that help and the words that wound, see What not to say to someone who is hurting, and what to say instead.

articles.title: What not to say to someone who is hurting, and what to say instead
sources: FEMA, CERT Basic Training Participant Manual (2019), Unit 5, "Disaster Psychology"
U.S. Army, ATP 4-02.11 First Aid (March 2026), chapter 20, "Combat and Operational Stress Control"
SAMHSA, "Tips for Talking With and Helping Children and Youth Cope After a Disaster or Traumatic Event: A Guide for Parents, Caregivers, and Teachers" (PEP23-01-01-012)
guidance: Some of the things we say to comfort people do the opposite. FEMA trains its volunteer responders to avoid these: "I understand" (unless you have lived the same thing, you cannot); "Don't feel bad" (they have a right to feel bad, and will need time to feel differently); "You're strong" or "You'll get through this" (many do not feel strong, and doubt they will recover); "Don't cry" (it is fine to cry); "It's God's will" (with someone you do not know well, giving the event a religious meaning can insult or anger them); and "It could be worse", "At least you still have…", or "Everything will be okay" (whether it could be worse, and whether it will be okay, is theirs to decide).

From the Army's first aid manual, three more that feel like help and land as hostility: "It's all in your head", "Snap out of it", and "Get control of yourself". They show a lack of understanding and only emphasise that the person is failing. Joking, indifference, and fearful or tearful attention do no better.

Say this instead: "I'm sorry for your pain." "I'm so sorry this has happened." "Is it all right if I help you with…?" "I can't imagine what this is like for you." "What do you need?" Ask permission before you step into their space, touch them, or start helping, and let them say what they need rather than deciding it for them.

Do not assume you know what someone is thinking or feeling; you cannot. Listen for the meaning behind the words, watch the face, the body, and the tone of voice, and every so often say back what you have heard, so they know you are following.
Silence is allowed. Do not say something just to relieve your own discomfort. And if something you said lands badly, it is fine to apologise.
Do not take what they say, or how they act, personally. The responses you see are part of what the event did to them, and almost never about anything you did or did not do.

With a child: get down to their eye level, use a calm, gentle voice and words they understand, and tell them you still care for them and will keep taking care of them. See Helping a frightened or crying child, by age.

articles.title: Someone who is frozen, dazed, wandering, or out of control
sources: U.S. Army, ATP 4-02.11 First Aid (March 2026), chapter 20, "Combat and Operational Stress Control"
FEMA, CERT Basic Training Participant Manual (2019), Unit 5, "Disaster Psychology"
guidance: Overwhelming stress can produce a person who cannot function: someone who freezes completely, who stands up or runs about in the open without purpose, who cannot follow a simple instruction, or who is so confused that their judgment is gone and they do not know what they are doing. In others it produces the opposite: constant movement, flinching or ducking at every sudden sound, shaking of the whole body, fast or nonsensical talk, arguing, reckless actions, indifference to danger, rapid swings of emotion, hysterical outbursts, or strange, frantic behaviour.

Some signs are stranger still, and are still stress: a person who cannot use an arm, a hand, or a leg with nothing physically wrong with it; who cannot see, hear, or feel; who cannot speak, or stutters or mumbles severely; who staggers and sways with a vacant stare; who sees or hears things that are not there; or who has lost their memory. These come on top of the ordinary signs of strain, and they usually improve quickly with reassurance, rest, food and water, and things that restore confidence.

Dazed, wandering, confused, or missing memory can also be a head injury, and the two can look the same. When nobody saw what happened and can say for certain that the person was not struck, treat it as a head injury until proven otherwise (see Head, neck and spinal injury): keep them from wandering into further danger, and get them to medical care by whatever route actually works.

If their behaviour endangers them or anyone else, do what is necessary to control them. Talk them into cooperating, calmly, first. Take away anything they could hurt themselves or others with, a firearm included, if you are seriously concerned about them. Physically restrain them only when it is needed for safety or to move them. A person who has panicked is likely to argue: respect their feelings, do not argue back, and point them at what needs doing right now.

Then reassure everyone around, the person included, that the signs are almost certainly stress and will improve quickly. Get them to a safer, quieter place. Do not leave them alone; keep someone they know with them. Have them looked at by medical people when that becomes possible. When they are not sleeping, eating, or resting, give them easy tasks, expect them to be back to themselves within about a day, and let them return to normal as soon as they are ready.

Panic is catching. One person running or screaming can set off the rest, so if you cannot get them interested in useful work, get help to contain them and keep them apart from the group until they settle. Give the steady, uninjured people jobs; it helps them too.
Afterward, see Calming someone who is falling apart: psychological first aid for the listening, the routine, and the rest that let a person come back.

articles.title: When someone says they want to die
sources: NIMH (National Institute of Mental Health), "5 Action Steps to Help Someone Having Thoughts of Suicide" (2024)
U.S. Navy, Hospital Corpsman (NAVEDTRA 14295), chapter 4, "Psychiatric emergencies"
VA National Center for PTSD, "Common Reactions After Trauma"
FEMA, CERT Basic Training Participant Manual (2019), Unit 5, "Disaster Psychology"
SAMHSA, "Tips for Survivors: Coping With Grief After a Disaster or Traumatic Event" (SMA17-5035)
guidance: Always take it as real. A suicide threat can be words, a gesture, or an attempt, and the Navy teaches its corpsmen to assume every one of them is real. Do not leave the person alone. The job, above everything else, is to keep them from harming themselves and to get them to a trained professional. In a disaster, that means by whatever route actually works: call if you have signal, otherwise get them there or send someone.

Ask, plainly: "Are you thinking about suicide?" It is a hard question to ask. Asking it does not put the idea in their head and does not increase the risk; studies show it does not, and it starts the conversation that can help.

Be there. Listen without judgment. Let them say what they are thinking and feeling; acknowledging it and talking about it may reduce the thoughts, not feed them. Trauma and loss can push someone who is already low toward thoughts of hurting themselves, and after a disaster that is not rare.

Help keep them safe. Ask whether they have a plan. Then make the means less available or less deadly: firearms locked away or held by someone else, medicines out of reach, and the person kept away from any place they have named. Reducing access to the most lethal means helps a person stay safe when the thoughts come.

Help them connect. With signal, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline takes calls and texts at 988, and the Disaster Distress Helpline, call or text 1-800-985-5990, is there for exactly this kind of week. Without signal, the connection is a trusted family member, a friend, a faith leader, or anyone in the group they will talk to; a person is a safety net too. Do not leave them without one.

Follow up. Staying in touch after the crisis, checking in the next day and the days after, makes a difference: supportive, ongoing contact plays a real part in preventing suicide. In a household riding out an emergency, that means someone keeps them in view and keeps talking with them.

If they have hurt themselves, treat the injury like any other and keep them with you. If they have swallowed something, do not make them vomit if they are not fully awake and alert; see Unknown swallowed poison, no induced vomiting and Non-opioid medication overdose. A calm, steady, understanding manner that does not agitate them is the first aid for almost every mental health emergency. Often it is a family member or friend who noticed the change and came for help; keep them part of it.

articles.title: Stress reactions after a disaster: what is normal, what helps, and when to get help
sources: SAMHSA, "Tips for Survivors of a Disaster or Other Traumatic Event: Managing Stress" (SMA13-4776)
VA National Center for PTSD, "Common Reactions After Trauma"
VA National Center for PTSD, "Coping with Traumatic Stress Reactions"
NIMH (National Institute of Mental Health), "Coping With Traumatic Events"
guidance: You do not have to have been hurt, or to have lost someone, to be affected by a disaster; seeing it is enough. Right after, most people feel relief to be alive, and then the stress, the fear, and the anger arrive, along with an inability to stop thinking about it and a body that stays on guard, reacting hard to every sound and sight. These reactions are common in everyone, trained responders included.

Stress shows up in four places. Feelings: anxious, fearful, overwhelmed by sadness, angry (especially if violence was involved), guilty even with no control over what happened, heroic as if you can do anything, too much energy or none at all, disconnected, numb. Body: stomach aches or diarrhoea, headaches and pains with no cause, eating too much or too little, sweating or chills, shaking or twitching, being jumpy and easily startled.

Behaviour: trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much; crying a lot; reaching for alcohol, tobacco, drugs, or extra medication to dull it; outbursts of anger and blaming everyone; difficulty accepting help or giving it; wanting to be alone. Thinking: trouble remembering, concentrating, and deciding; confusion; constant worry; difficulty talking about what happened or listening to others.

The first tasks, in order: make sure you are not injured, because people often do not notice for hours; if you are, get treated before anything else. Find a safe place to stay. Let a family member or friend know where you are and how to reach you. Secure your identification and papers: insurance, bank, property, medical records. Then list the most important things to do and do them one at a time; each finished task gives back a little control. Take a few deep breaths, or a gentle stretch, before each one, and plan something restful after a stretch of work.

What helps most people: talk with others who understand and accept how you feel, a trusted friend, family member, or faith leader, and other survivors. Move the body every day, even a walk or stretching, to burn off the stress hormones, but do not lift heavy weights while the adrenaline is high, because it can damage muscle. Breathe deeply, often. Listen to music. Sleep and rest every day, eat properly, drink plenty of water, and go easy on caffeine, tobacco, and alcohol, whose effects are multiplied under stress. Use whatever got you through hard times before.

For the pounding heart and the sudden panic: they usually come from fast breathing, they are not dangerous, and slowing the breath helps; the frightening thoughts that ride along, "I'm going to die", are not true (see Panic attack or anxiety attack: what it feels like, what to do, and when it is something else). For a flashback: keep your eyes open, look around and say where you are and what year it is, get up and move, drink some water and wash your hands, and tell someone you trust what is happening. For a nightmare: remind yourself you are reacting to a dream, not to danger now; get up, regroup, and do something calming. For anger: take a time-out and walk away, and if you blow up at someone, talk to them about it as soon as you can. For a mind that will not focus: slow down, write things down, break jobs into small pieces, and plan a realistic day.

Sleep: keep a regular bedtime; no heavy exertion in the few hours before it; no alcohol, tobacco, or caffeine; and do not lie there worrying, get up and do something quiet and pleasant until you are sleepy.

Distressing feelings usually fade over 2 to 4 weeks as routines come back, especially for people who have done some of the above. Get help, when help can be reached, if the reactions are not easing, are getting worse, or are getting in the way of relationships, work, or daily life; if there is depression (down more days than not, no interest in anything, hopeless); if you are blaming yourself for surviving or for what you did or did not do; if anger is turning into violence; if drinking or drugs are taking over; or if there are any thoughts of suicide. See When someone says they want to die.
Children react differently, and often later; see Helping a frightened or crying child, by age.

articles.title: Grief after a disaster: what is normal, and when it has become stuck
sources: SAMHSA, "Tips for Survivors: Coping With Grief After a Disaster or Traumatic Event" (SMA17-5035)
MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine), "Bereavement" health topic
FEMA, CERT Basic Training Participant Manual (2019), Unit 5, "Disaster Psychology"
guidance: Grief is the normal response of sorrow, heartache, and confusion to losing someone or something important, and a disaster brings many losses at once: people, homes, possessions, and the feeling that the world is safe. It can feel like emptiness and numbness, an inability to feel joy or sadness, or anger. The body may tremble or shake, feel weak, lose its appetite, feel sick, struggle to sleep or to breathe, or have a dry mouth. Nightmares, pulling away from people, and not wanting to do the usual things are all part of it.

Grief is different for every person and every loss. How the person died, how close you were, whether it was expected, and your own circumstances all change how long it lasts. Right now it may be impossible to imagine the pain ending. It will ease. Life may not be the same, but grieving is what lets you accept the loss and go on.

What helps: talking to people who understand and respect how you feel, family, faith leaders, people you trust; taking care of the body with some exercise, proper meals, and enough sleep; and allowing yourself to feel both joy and sadness, and to cry when you need to. Friends, family, and faith are sources of support, and grief counselling helps some people.

Healing does not mean forgetting. You can stay deeply connected to the person you lost and still come to imagine a life without them, re-enter daily life, and reconnect with others. Moving out of grief looks like feeling the pain without resisting or avoiding it, adjusting to a reality in which they are not present, and forming new relationships. Some people later notice they have become more understanding and tolerant, more grateful for the people around them, more spiritually connected, more socially active.

A disaster can jam the process. Sorrow and anger about the home and possessions pile on top of the death, fear about safety sits underneath, and simply meeting the day's needs can push grieving aside, which can delay, prolong, or complicate it. For most people the intense feelings begin to ease within about 6 months. If after many months you feel stuck in deep and overwhelming loss, or the sadness, anger, and loneliness are getting stronger rather than weaker, it may have become complicated or traumatic grief.

The signs of stuck grief: deep anger about the death; being unable to think about anything but the person; wanting no reminders of them at all; nightmares or intrusive thoughts; deep loneliness and longing; distrust of others; being unable to keep up ordinary activities or responsibilities; bitterness about life and envy of people untouched by grief; being unable to enjoy anything or to remember happy times with them. Any of these is a reason to get help, from a doctor or another health professional, when one can be reached.

Where to turn, with signal: the Disaster Distress Helpline, call or text 1-800-985-5990, around the clock; SAMHSA's National Helpline, 1-800-662-4357; and for anyone who is thinking of suicide, call or text 988. Without signal, the people around you are the help, and the listening in Calming someone who is falling apart: psychological first aid is how they give it.
If someone dies in your care: cover the body and treat it with respect, and follow local rules for the dead. The people who were there will need someone to listen in the days after.

articles.title: Helping a frightened or crying child, by age
sources: SAMHSA, "Tips for Talking With and Helping Children and Youth Cope After a Disaster or Traumatic Event: A Guide for Parents, Caregivers, and Teachers" (PEP23-01-01-012)
NIMH (National Institute of Mental Health), "Coping With Traumatic Events"
guidance: A son or daughter of any age can be shaken by a disaster they lived through, one they watched on a screen, or one they overheard adults discussing. They react differently from adults, some at once and some much later, so the adults do not always know when a child needs help. Most of the reactions below are normal in the first weeks. If one lasts more than 2 to 4 weeks, or appears out of nowhere later, the child needs more help than they are getting.

Babies and toddlers (0 to 2) cannot understand what is happening, but they know when their caregiver is upset and often mirror it: crying for no reason, withdrawing, not playing with their toys. Preschoolers (3 to 5) may go back to thumb-sucking or wetting the bed, fear the dark, strangers, or monsters, cling, want to stay where they feel safe, act out the event over and over in play or tell exaggerated stories about it, eat and sleep differently, complain of aches with no cause, or turn aggressive, withdrawn, hyperactive, or disobedient. Forgetting how to talk is another sign in the youngest.

Children 6 to 10 may be afraid to go to school, drop their friends, lose the ability to pay attention, become aggressive for no clear reason, or act younger, asking to be fed or dressed. Teens and older youth (11 to 19) often deny it: a routine "I'm okay", silence, physical aches they cannot explain, arguments at home and at school, resistance to any rule, and sometimes alcohol, drugs, or other risks. Older children may also feel guilty for not having prevented harm, or think about revenge.

Adult support and reassurance is the key, and children are usually resilient: with it, most are themselves again soon. What matters most is that a child feels connected, cared about, and loved. Let them express it in talk, writing, drawing, and singing. Most children want to talk about what happened, so let them, and accept the feelings: it is okay to feel sad, upset, or stressed, and crying relieves stress and grief. Pay attention and listen well. Do not pressure a child to talk or to join in; some are frightened all over again by talking about it, listening to it, or looking at drawings of it, and they should be free to step away.

With a little one: take a deep breath before you pick them up, and focus on them, not on the disaster. Get down to their eye level and speak in a calm, gentle voice, in words they understand. Tell them you still care for them and will keep taking care of them, so that they feel safe. Cuddle them a lot.

With an older child or a teen: ask what worries them and what might help. Offer comfort with gentle words, a hug when it is welcome, or just your presence. Spend more time with them than usual, even short stretches. Excuse them from chores for a day or two, then give them age-appropriate tasks so they feel useful; helping others is one of the ways children cope, whether a thank-you note to someone who helped or a letter to someone who lost their home. Let them see friends, have quiet time to write or draw, and move around and play. Get routines back, and school when it exists again.

Ask what they have heard and seen. Watch the coverage with them, then limit it so they have time away from reminders, and do not let the disaster take over every conversation. Answer their questions. Point to the good in it: the heroic actions, the neighbours and families who helped. If a person or a mistake caused the event, do not blame a race, a culture, or people with mental illness, and make sure the child knows they are not to blame when bad things happen.

Children can see you sad or crying; that is fine. Screaming, hitting or kicking walls or furniture, or any violence is not; it frightens them and can add to the harm. Never hit, isolate, abandon, or make fun of a child who is struggling. Look after your own reactions in a healthy way and let them see you do it: routines, meals, sleep, exercise, and deep breaths, because an adult who is coping is an adult who is available.
See also Helping children cope with disaster stress and Family reunification if separated.

articles.title: Taking care of yourself while you take care of everyone else
sources: FEMA, CERT Basic Training Participant Manual (2019), Unit 5, "Disaster Psychology"
SAMHSA, "Tips for Survivors of a Disaster or Other Traumatic Event: Managing Stress" (SMA13-4776)
U.S. Army, ATP 4-02.11 First Aid (March 2026), chapter 20, "Combat and Operational Stress Control"
guidance: The person holding everyone together gets hurt too. Dealing with your own losses, working in your own neighbourhood, helping injured neighbours and friends, and feeling unsafe all produce normal stress reactions in rescuers. There is a second kind as well: taking on a survivor's feelings as your own, called vicarious trauma or compassion fatigue, which sets in when you identify too closely with someone you are helping. It can leave you unable to do the job well.

Watch yourself for the same signs you would watch for in anyone: no appetite, headaches or chest pain, stomach trouble, restlessness, drinking or using more, nightmares, no sleep, exhaustion, and on the inside a loss of hope, despair, asking "why me", and a sense that nothing you do is enough.

Only you know what lowers your stress, and the time to work that out is before the bad week, not during it. The basics: enough sleep, regular exercise, a balanced diet, a balance of work, play, and rest, connection with other people, and whatever spiritual resource is yours. Allow yourself to receive as well as give; you are more than a helper.

Tell the people close to you how to support you: listen when you want to talk, and do not push you to talk before you are ready. Share with them what the stress reactions look like, so they know what they are seeing.

If you are leading a group: tell people beforehand what they are likely to see and how they and the survivors may react; share the workload and the emotional load; make people rest and take breaks away from the scene before they are worn out; and make it normal to talk about what happened.

The Army's version: physical exhaustion is often the real cause of an emotional collapse, so a sleep plan, a safe, dry, quiet place to sleep, and the chance to wash and put on clean, dry clothes are not luxuries; they are what keep people functioning. A tight-knit group carries its members: everyone works, faces danger, and handles trouble better inside one.

After a stretch of hard work, do something restful on purpose. Move the body daily to clear the stress hormones, but do not lift heavy weights while the adrenaline is up. Breathe deeply and often; see Slow breathing: the calming exercise for stress, anxiety, and panic.
